```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

source("ps2_script_khogali.R")
```

## Data

These are seasonally adjusted monthly unemployment rates for the
United States, Oregon, California, Texas, and New York. The data
come from FRED and are saved locally.

```{r}
unemp_raw <- read_rds("data/unemp_raw.rds")

knitr::kable(
  head(unemp_raw),
  caption = "First six rows of the data"
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

cat(
  "The sample covers",
  format(min(unemp_raw$date), "%B %Y"),
  "through",
  paste0(format(max(unemp_raw$date), "%B %Y"), ".")
)
```

## Wrangling

I renamed the rate column and added region names. Following the
instructions, I replaced October 2025 rates with September's values.
I also calculated each region's monthly change in percentage points.

### Full sample

Mean, minimum, and maximum unemployment rates for each region:

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  unemp_summary,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Region", "Mean (%)", "Minimum (%)", "Maximum (%)")
)
```

### January 2015 onward

The same statistics for the more recent period:

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  unemp_recent_summary,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Region", "Mean (%)", "Minimum (%)", "Maximum (%)")
)
```

### Largest increases excluding 2020

The five largest monthly increases, including ties. Changes are
measured in percentage points.

```{r}
unemp_top_increases_no_covid |>
  select(region, date, unemployment_rate, unemployment_rate_change) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Region", "Month", "Rate (%)", "Change (pp)")
  )
```

### Largest decreases excluding 2020

The five largest monthly decreases, including ties. Negative values
mean unemployment fell.

```{r}
unemp_top_decreases_no_covid |>
  select(region, date, unemployment_rate, unemployment_rate_change) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Region", "Month", "Rate (%)", "Change (pp)")
  )
```

## Visualization

### Unemployment by region

This graph compares all five regions over time.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5

plot_all
```

### Separate region graphs

Separate panels make each region easier to follow. They use the
same scale for comparison.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

plot_facets
```

### Average unemployment

Regions are ordered from lowest to highest average unemployment
over the full sample.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

plot_means
```

### Oregon and the United States

I chose to compare Oregon with the national rate since 2015 because
I wanted to see how unemployment here compares with the country overall.
Using just two lines makes the differences easier to see.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5

plot_oregon_us
```

## Reflection

I used AI to teach me how to write some code and trouble shoot the code I was writing initially. But making the graphs was simple once I had the data ready. I wasn't sure when to run each block of code. I also had trouble with Git because I hadn't saved my changes before trying to commit them. I learned that saving, committing, and pushing are separate steps. I feel more comfortable using Git now and checking that my work shows up on GitHub.
